newText: Memory hooks: if you already know these events and their dates, the number connects to knowledge you already have. If the events are unfamiliar, this particular connection will be less useful to you, even though the grouping and date structure may still help.

What changed is our interpretation, or framing, of the information, which makes it easier to remember due to 3 concepts:
[AUTHOR INSTRUCTION] REVEAL MEMORY-PRINCIPLES: start with all three principles hidden. Each learner click on “Show the next idea” reveals one complete principle in order: Chunking, Logical constraints, Memory hooks. Bold each title. Keep earlier principles visible; after the third, remove the reveal control and offer Continue. No automatic advance or animation timer. Use a native button, announce each new item, retain keyboard focus and respect reduced motion.

oldText: All three principles will come back throughout the course. If you’re interested, the section below explains in more detail how these principles work.
newText: All three principles will come back throughout the course. Let’s check what they mean in practice.

oldText:
[PLACEHOLDER / AUTHOR INSTRUCTION] OPTIONAL SLIDE-DOWN MEMORY-ASSOCIATIVE-NETWORK: collapsed by default, labelled “How does the associative network memory model explain this?” Open and close on request; opening it is not required for progress and adds no quiz. Keep focus on the control, expose its expanded/collapsed state, and respect reduced motion.
OPTIONAL LEARNER TEXT: One useful way to think about memory is as a network of connected ideas. Bringing one idea to mind can make related ideas easier to reach. For example, thinking about American Independence Day may bring July 4 to mind, which then helps you recover part of the number. In an associative network model, those links help explain how one idea can lead to another. We’ll use connections like these to give new Hebrew material a familiar starting point.

oldText: LEARNER PROMPT: Match each observation to the principle that explains it.
newText: LEARNER PROMPT: Imagine you recognise the number as two dates, but neither event is familiar to you. What could still help you remember it?

oldText: OBSERVATIONS:
newText: OPTIONS:

oldText: 1. Thinking of two dates instead of sixteen separate digits.
newText: A. Memorise the names of the three memory principles.

oldText: 2. Ruling out 19 as the month because a year has only twelve months.
newText: B. Use the two date groups and what you know about how dates work.

oldText: 3. Using your existing knowledge of American Independence Day to recover July 4.
newText: C. Attach an event name to each date, even if neither event means anything to you.

oldText:
RESPONSE OPTIONS (each used once):
A. Logical constraints
B. Connecting new information to established old information
C. Chunking
ANSWER / ACCEPTED MODEL: 1 → C (Chunking); 2 → A (Logical constraints); 3 → B (Connecting new information to established old information).
newText: ANSWER / ACCEPTED MODEL: B. Use the two date groups and what you know about how dates work.

oldText: FEEDBACK for observation 1: “Chunking. You’re grouping the digits into two larger units.”
newText: FEEDBACK after A: “Knowing the names doesn’t help you recover these digits. Try using the grouping and date structure instead.”

oldText: FEEDBACK for observation 2: “Logical constraints. Knowing how months work rules out an impossible value.”
newText: FEEDBACK after B: “Yes. Two date groups give you larger units to work with, and the date format limits the possibilities. Those can still help even when the events are unfamiliar.”

oldText: FEEDBACK for observation 3: “Connecting new information to established old information. Something you already know helps you recover the date.”
newText: FEEDBACK after C: “An unfamiliar event name adds something else to remember. A useful memory hook connects the new information to something you already know.”

newText: [AUTHOR INSTRUCTION] This is the only comprehension question in the lesson. It checks how the ideas work, not recall of their names. Show the authored feedback for the selected option and the explanation for B after submission. Permit Continue without a compulsory repeat round.
